title: Using ChatGPT as a Lesson Planning Assistant with Preservice Secondary Mathematics Teachers
extended_summary:
This qualitative study examines how preservice secondary mathematics teachers used ChatGPT as a lesson-planning assistant during a methods course microteaching assignment. The paper focuses on two related questions: how preservice teachers reacted to ChatGPT’s mathematical output and what they found useful or not useful when using the chatbot to plan a mini-lesson. The authors frame the work around reflective teaching practice, arguing that successful use of generative AI in lesson planning depends on critical evaluation rather than blind acceptance of generated output.

The intervention consisted of having 22 preservice teachers first solve a mathematics task and draft lesson aims/objectives on their own, then ask ChatGPT to solve the same task and help generate lesson-planning components. Over several weeks, participants could continue using ChatGPT informally while preparing a mini-lesson for a secondary mathematics methods course. Data came from written reflections, lesson-planning artifacts, and comparisons of the preservice teachers’ and ChatGPT’s mathematical solutions. The sample included 17 undergraduate students and 5 graduate career-changers at a public urban university in the northeastern United States.

Findings showed that participants were generally better at judging the pedagogical usefulness of ChatGPT than its mathematical correctness. They often found ChatGPT helpful for generating aims, objectives, outlines, prior knowledge prompts, misconceptions, and other planning ideas, but judged many outputs as teacher-centered, repetitive, or overly generic. Although ChatGPT’s mathematical solutions were often incorrect, most preservice teachers failed to recognize those errors and instead described them as alternative approaches. The study concludes that ChatGPT can serve as a limited brainstorming aid in lesson planning, but preservice teachers need explicit support in critique, reflection, and mathematical verification.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative descriptive study with a convenience sample of 22 preservice teachers and no experimental comparison, so it provides only low-to-moderate causal credibility. It is still peer-reviewed research evidence, but it is primarily interpretive rather than causal.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests practical usefulness for lesson-planning support and documents substantial math errors, but it reports no quantitative effect sizes and no direct learner outcomes. The impact is therefore modest and unclear for K-12 practice, especially since the sample is preservice-adjacent rather than in-service teachers or students.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT as a lesson-planning assistant for preservice secondary mathematics teachers to generate lesson ideas, aims/objectives, sample solutions, misconceptions, assessments, and general planning support during microteaching preparation.

finding.finding_summary: This qualitative study found that preservice teachers often used ChatGPT as a starting point for lesson planning and reflected critically on its outputs, showing some metacognitive evaluation of pedagogy and content. However, they were much less accurate in judging ChatGPT’s mathematical correctness: only 1 of 19 coded instances involved a PST correctly identifying ChatGPT’s incorrect math output, while 13 of 19 ChatGPT solutions were incorrect overall.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of reflective statements about ChatGPT’s output, including whether PSTs identified errors and how they evaluated usefulness
finding.study_size: n=22 PSTs; 19 coded PST-ChatGPT problem-solving instances

finding.finding_summary: PSTs reported that ChatGPT was helpful for generating structured outlines, objectives, prior knowledge prompts, misconceptions, and some assessment ideas, suggesting it could save planning time and provide a useful starting point. At the same time, they often judged the output to be repetitive, teacher-centered, or not directly usable, so the efficiency benefit was limited and required substantial human revision.
finding.measure: Qualitative reflections on usefulness/not usefulness of ChatGPT for lesson planning

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT frequently produced incorrect mathematical solutions in the lesson-planning tasks. Across 19 coded problem instances, ChatGPT was correct only 6 times and incorrect 13 times; in 10 of the 19 instances, the PST solved the problem correctly while ChatGPT did not, and only 1 PST accurately identified ChatGPT’s incorrect math output.
finding.measure: Correctness of solutions to mathematics problems embedded in lesson-planning tasks
finding.study_size: n=19 coded PST-ChatGPT problem instances (from n=22 PSTs)
